lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Preparing Feed for Domestic and Commercial Animals

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Demonstrate how farmers prepare feed for different domestic and commercial animals with ingredients.
- Write down the process of preparing feed for different domestic and commercial animals with the ingredients.
- Compile a table matching feed, ingredients and method of preparation.
- Formulate and prepare feed for domestic and commercial animals.

pages.title: Why Prepared Feed Matters
pages.body: Domestic animals, such as those kept for household use, and commercial animals, raised at a larger scale for sale, both depend on properly prepared feed to grow well, remain healthy, and produce meat, milk or eggs efficiently. Preparing feed deliberately, using known ingredients and a consistent method, allows a farmer to control the quality and balance of nutrients an animal receives, rather than relying only on whatever happens to be available.

questions.q: Prepared animal feed mainly allows a farmer to
o: Control the quality and balance of nutrients an animal receives
Increase the animal's need for water only
Prevent the animal from growing at all
Remove all responsibility for animal care
questions.e: Preparing feed deliberately, using known ingredients and a consistent method, allows a farmer to control the quality and balance of nutrients an animal receives, rather than relying only on whatever happens to be available.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Common Prepared Feeds, Their Ingredients and Preparation

pages.title: Common Prepared Feeds, Their Ingredients and Preparation
pages.body:
Poultry mash, silage, fish meal supplement and kitchen or farm waste feed are four commonly prepared animal feeds, each requiring specific ingredients and a specific method of preparation, as summarised in the table below.

| **FEED TYPE** | **INGREDIENTS** | **METHOD OF PREPARATION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Poultry mash** | Maize bran, fish meal, soybean meal, oyster shell, vitamin premix, salt | Weigh each ingredient according to the required proportion, mix thoroughly until evenly combined, and store in a dry, sealed container |
| **Silage (for cattle)** | Chopped green maize or grass, sometimes with added molasses | Chop plant material finely, pack tightly into an airtight pit or bag to remove air, and allow to ferment for several weeks before feeding |
| **Fish meal supplement** | Dried, ground fish or fish waste | Dry fish thoroughly under the sun or in a dryer, then grind into a fine meal and mix into other feed as a protein source |
| **Kitchen and farm waste feed (for pigs)** | Vegetable peelings, leftover food, crop residues | Collect and sort waste materials, chop larger pieces, and boil where necessary to soften and reduce the risk of disease before feeding |

[[pic:A step by step illustrated sequence showing poultry mash preparation, first a set of labelled ingredient containers (maize bran, fish meal, soybean meal, oyster shell), then a person weighing ingredients on a scale, then the same person mixing them thoroughly in a large basin, and finally the finished mash being poured into a sealed storage container.]]

Notice how feed preparation generally follows a similar overall pattern, gathering the correct ingredients, measuring them accurately, combining or processing them appropriately, and then storing the finished feed properly, even though the specific ingredients and processing steps differ from one feed type to another.

pages.title: General Steps in Preparing Animal Feed
pages.body: Selecting ingredients, measuring proportions, combining or processing the ingredients, and storing the finished feed are four general steps that apply across most feed preparation methods, regardless of the specific feed being made. Selecting the right ingredients means choosing materials that supply the nutrients a particular animal needs, considering factors such as protein, energy, minerals and vitamins. Measuring proportions accurately ensures the feed is properly balanced rather than accidentally too rich in one nutrient and deficient in another. Combining or processing the ingredients, whether through simple mixing, chopping, drying, grinding or fermenting, prepares the feed in a form the animal can eat and digest easily. Storing the finished feed correctly, usually in a dry, sealed, pest free container, protects it from spoiling or losing nutritional value before it is used.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Formulating Feed for a Specific Animal

pages.title: Formulating Feed for a Specific Animal
pages.body: Formulating feed means deliberately calculating and combining ingredients to meet the specific nutritional needs of a particular animal at a particular stage of growth, rather than simply mixing whatever ingredients are available. A farmer formulating feed for laying hens, for example, needs to include enough calcium to support strong eggshells, alongside adequate protein and energy, while feed formulated for a young, growing pig needs to emphasise protein for muscle development. Learning to formulate feed thoughtfully, rather than by guesswork, is an important skill for anyone hoping to raise healthy, productive animals efficiently.

pages.title: Formulating a Feed, a Worked Example
pages.body:
To formulate a feed means to work out how much of each ingredient to mix so that the feed has the right proportion of a nutrient, usually protein. A simple method for two ingredients is the square method, often called the Pearson square. Suppose a farmer wants 100 kg of feed with 18 percent protein from maize, which has about 9 percent protein, and soya bean meal, which has about 44 percent protein.

| **STEP** | **WORKING** | **RESULT** |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Find the parts of maize** | Protein in soya bean meal minus the protein wanted, which is 44 minus 18 | 26 parts of maize |
| **2. Find the parts of soya bean meal** | Protein wanted minus the protein in maize, which is 18 minus 9 | 9 parts of soya bean meal |
| **3. Add the parts** | 26 plus 9 | 35 parts in all |
| **4. Change the parts to kilograms in 100 kg** | Maize is 26 divided by 35, multiplied by 100. Soya bean meal is 9 divided by 35, multiplied by 100 | About 74 kg of maize and about 26 kg of soya bean meal |
| **5. Check** | 74 kg of maize gives about 6.7 kg of protein and 26 kg of soya bean meal gives about 11.4 kg | About 18 kg of protein in 100 kg, which is 18 percent |

The method works only when the protein wanted lies between the protein levels of the two ingredients. After the main ingredients are worked out, small amounts of oyster shell, salt and vitamin premix are added. Ingredients are weighed, ground where necessary, mixed from the smallest amount to the largest so that they spread evenly, and stored in dry bags.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Commercial feed mills use precise formulas, often developed by animal nutritionists, and industrial equipment to prepare large quantities of consistent, balanced feed for sale to farmers. Understanding the basic principles of feed preparation studied in this lesson provides a foundation for appreciating how these larger scale, more technical feed production systems work, even though a smallholder farmer may prepare feed using much simpler tools and smaller quantities.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Selecting Appropriate Feed for Different Animals

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Compile a list of feed commonly consumed by the different domestic and commercial animals in the environment.
- Compare and contrast the characteristics of different kinds of feed commonly consumed by categories of domestic and commercial animals, namely ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.
- Record feed used to feed domestic and commercial animals on farms over a period of time.
- Identify named samples of feed for three categories of domestic and commercial animals, namely ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.

pages.title: Categories of Domestic and Commercial Animals
pages.body: Ruminants, monogastrics and poultry are three broad categories used to classify domestic and commercial animals based mainly on their digestive system, and this classification strongly influences the type of feed each category can process efficiently.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a monogastric animal?

pages.title: Ruminants and Their Feed
pages.body: A ruminant is an animal with a specialised, multi chambered stomach that allows it to digest large amounts of fibrous plant material efficiently, through a process involving regurgitating and re chewing partly digested food, commonly called chewing the cud. Cattle, goats and sheep are common ruminants kept in Ghana. Ruminants feed mainly on roughage, such as grass, hay, maize stalks and other fibrous crop residues, since their specialised stomach allows them to extract nutrients from this fibrous material far more effectively than other animals can.

pages.title: Monogastrics and Their Feed
pages.body: A monogastric animal has a single chambered stomach, similar in basic structure to the human stomach, which cannot break down fibrous plant material as efficiently as a ruminant's stomach can. Pigs are the most common monogastric livestock kept in Ghana. Monogastrics feed mainly on concentrates, energy and protein rich feeds such as maize bran, soybean meal and kitchen or farm waste, since their simpler digestive system needs feed that is already easier to break down and absorb.

questions.q: Ruminant animals are best described as having
o: A specialised, multi chambered stomach for digesting fibrous material
The same digestive system as poultry
questions.e: A ruminant is an animal with a specialised, multi chambered stomach that allows it to digest large amounts of fibrous plant material efficiently, through a process involving regurgitating and re chewing partly digested food, commonly called chewing the cud.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a ruminant?
questions.e: Cattle, goats and sheep are common ruminants kept in Ghana.

questions.e: Ruminants feed mainly on roughage, such as grass, hay, maize stalks and other fibrous crop residues, since their specialised stomach allows them to extract nutrients from this fibrous material far more effectively than other animals can.

o: The same stomach structure as a ruminant
questions.e: A monogastric animal has a single chambered stomach, similar in basic structure to the human stomach, which cannot break down fibrous plant material as efficiently as a ruminant's stomach can.

pages.title: Poultry and Their Feed
pages.body:
Poultry, including chickens, guinea fowl and ducks, also have a simple digestive system, supported by a muscular organ called the gizzard that helps grind food, sometimes with the help of small stones the bird deliberately swallows. Poultry feed mainly on concentrated feed such as maize bran, fish meal and formulated poultry mash, alongside mineral supplements such as oyster shell to support eggshell formation in laying birds.

[[pic:A three column comparison chart with labelled photographs or drawings, one column showing a cow grazing on grass under the heading Ruminant, one column showing a pig eating from a trough of mixed feed under the heading Monogastric, and one column showing chickens pecking at grain and mash under the heading Poultry, with the main feed type listed beneath each image.]]

Notice how the type of feed each animal category consumes is closely matched to what its digestive system can process efficiently, which is why understanding an animal's digestive category is the first step in selecting appropriate feed for it.

pages.title: Comparing Feed Characteristics Across Categories
pages.body: Fibre content, energy content, and protein content are three characteristics that differ noticeably between the feeds typically given to ruminants, monogastrics and poultry. Ruminant feed, being mainly roughage, is generally high in fibre but relatively lower in concentrated energy and protein, which suits the ruminant's ability to extract nutrients slowly from large volumes of fibrous material over time. Monogastric and poultry feed, being mainly concentrates, is generally lower in fibre but higher in energy and protein, suited to a digestive system that processes feed more quickly and needs nutrients in a more readily available form.

pages.title: Recording Feed Use Over Time
pages.body: Recording the type and amount of feed given to farm animals over a period of time, such as daily or weekly, helps a farmer track feeding costs, monitor whether animals are receiving a consistent, balanced diet, and identify problems early if an animal's feed intake changes unexpectedly, which can sometimes be an early sign of illness.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Some feed ingredients, such as maize bran and fish meal, are used across more than one animal category, though usually in different proportions matched to each category's specific needs. Recognising this overlap can help a farmer manage feed purchasing and storage more efficiently across a mixed farm that keeps ruminants, monogastrics and poultry together.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Feed for Different Growth Stages of Animals

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Categorise different types of animals according to their stages of growth, namely young, growing and matured stages.
- List the types of feed used for the various stages of growth in domestic and commercial ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.
- Compare and construct the major functions of feed in each growth stage of different animals.
- Discuss types of feed used to feed different domestic and commercial animals at different stages of growth.

pages.title: Why Feed Needs Change as Animals Grow
pages.body: An animal's nutritional needs change considerably as it moves from a young, rapidly growing stage, through a growing stage, to full maturity, and, for many farm animals, into a productive stage where it supplies milk, eggs or offspring. Building on Lesson 9, which introduced ruminants, monogastrics and poultry as broad feeding categories, this lesson looks specifically at how feed should differ for the same animal at different points in its life.

questions.q: The underlying pattern across ruminants, monogastrics and poultry regarding growth stage feeding is that
o: All animals need identical feed regardless of stage
Nutritional needs change with growth stage across all these animal categories
Only poultry require different feed at different stages
Only ruminants require different feed at different stages
questions.e: Formulating feed means deliberately calculating and combining ingredients to meet the specific nutritional needs of a particular animal at a particular stage of growth, rather than simply mixing whatever ingredients are available.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Growth Stages and Their Feed Requirements

pages.title: Growth Stages and Their Feed Requirements
pages.body:
Young, growing, mature non producing, and mature producing are four general growth stages that apply, with some variation, across ruminants, monogastrics and poultry, each requiring a different feed emphasis, as summarised in the table below.

| **GROWTH STAGE** | **MAIN NUTRITIONAL NEED** | **TYPICAL FEED** | **REASON** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Young (for example chicks, calves, piglets)** | High protein for rapid tissue growth | Starter feed, high protein concentrate, milk (for mammals) | Young animals grow quickly and need extra protein to build new body tissue |
| **Growing** | Balanced protein and energy for continued development | Grower feed, a moderate protein concentrate mixed with some roughage | Growth continues steadily and needs a balanced supply of nutrients, not just protein alone |
| **Mature, non producing** | Moderate energy mainly for maintenance | Maintenance feed, mainly roughage with modest concentrate | A fully grown animal not producing milk, eggs or young needs less nutrient input, mainly to maintain its body |
| **Mature, producing (for example laying hens, dairy cows, pregnant animals)** | High energy, protein and minerals to support production | Layer feed or lactation feed with added calcium and other minerals | Producing eggs, milk or offspring places extra nutritional demand on the animal, beyond simple maintenance |

[[pic:A growth timeline diagram for a chicken, showing four labelled stages from left to right, a small chick eating starter feed, a growing pullet eating grower feed, and finally a fully grown laying hen eating layer feed with a visible egg beside her, with a short caption beneath each stage summarising its main feed need.]]

Notice how the type of feed changes at each stage to match the animal's changing needs, moving from a strong emphasis on protein while young, through a balanced feed while growing, to a feed enriched with minerals such as calcium once the animal begins laying eggs or producing milk.

pages.title: Feed Functions Across Growth Stages
pages.body: Building new body tissue, supporting steady growth, maintaining the body, and supporting production are four major functions feed can serve, and different growth stages rely on different combinations of these functions. Young animals rely heavily on feed to build new body tissue quickly, since their bodies are growing rapidly relative to their size. Growing animals continue to rely on tissue building, but increasingly need feed to support broader development, including bone and muscle growth, in a more balanced way. Mature, non producing animals mainly need feed to maintain their existing body condition, with lower overall nutrient demand than younger or producing animals. Mature, producing animals, such as laying hens or dairy cows, need feed that goes beyond simple maintenance, supplying the extra protein, energy and minerals needed to support egg, milk or offspring production.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Applying This Across Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry

pages.title: Applying This Across Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry
pages.body: A young calf, a young piglet and a young chick all need higher protein feed relative to their body size than their mature counterparts, even though the specific feed differs, milk and starter feed for the calf and piglet, and a fine, high protein starter mash for the chick. A mature dairy cow, a mature sow, and a mature laying hen all need extra nutrients to support production, though again the specific feed differs, a lactation ration rich in energy for the cow, a lactation feed for the sow, and a calcium enriched layer feed for the hen. Recognising this shared underlying pattern, even across very different animals, helps a farmer reason through appropriate feed choices for any animal at any stage, rather than needing to memorise every specific case separately.

pages.title: Feeds for Each Stage of Growth of Poultry, Pigs and Ruminants
pages.body:
| **ANIMAL** | **YOUNG STAGE** | **GROWING STAGE** | **MATURE OR PRODUCING STAGE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Layers** | Chick starter mash from day old to about 8 weeks, with about 20 percent protein | Grower mash from about 9 to 18 weeks, with less protein | Layer mash from the start of laying, with high calcium for eggshells |
| **Broilers** | Broiler starter for the first 3 to 4 weeks, with the highest protein | Broiler finisher from about 4 weeks | Sold for meat at about 6 to 8 weeks |
| **Pigs** | Milk of the sow, with creep feed offered from about 2 weeks until weaning at about 6 to 8 weeks | Weaner feed and then grower feed, rich in protein | Finisher feed for fattening, and a special ration for sows that are pregnant or nursing |
| **Cattle, sheep and goats** | Colostrum in the first days, then milk, with soft grass introduced gradually | Good pasture with some concentrate after weaning | Pasture, hay or silage, with concentrates for animals giving milk and a salt lick for all |

Colostrum is the first thick, yellowish milk a mother produces after giving birth. It is rich in protein and in antibodies that protect the newborn from disease, so every young mammal should receive it within the first hours of life. In general, young animals need the most protein for building tissue, growing animals need protein and energy, and mature animals need feed for maintenance, with extra nutrients when they are producing eggs, milk or young.

o: Only ruminants and never poultry or pigs

questions.e: Young animals, such as chicks or piglets, are typically fed smaller amounts more frequently throughout the day, since their small stomachs cannot hold a large single meal, while mature animals are usually fed larger amounts less frequently.

Overfeeding or underfeeding an animal relative to its growth stage can cause real problems, such as excessive fat deposits in an overfed, mature, non producing animal, or poor growth and weakened immunity in an underfed young animal. This is one reason commercial farms often follow carefully documented feeding schedules matched precisely to each growth stage, rather than feeding every animal on the farm the same way regardless of age or productive status.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Performing the Feeding of Domestic and Commercial Animals

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Demonstrate how to feed domestic and commercial animals at different stages of growth and production, with appropriate feed, in the school farm or a farm in the community.

pages.title: From Knowledge to Practice
pages.body: Lessons 8, 9 and 10 built up the knowledge needed to prepare feed, select feed suited to an animal's digestive category, and match feed to an animal's growth stage. This final lesson in the strand focuses on actually performing the feeding of animals correctly and safely, turning that accumulated knowledge into a practical, hands on skill.

pages.title: Preparing to Feed an Animal
pages.body: Confirming the correct feed, checking the correct quantity, and ensuring clean feeding equipment are three preparation steps that should happen before an animal is actually fed. Confirming the correct feed means checking that the feed matches both the animal's digestive category, ruminant, monogastric or poultry, and its specific growth stage, whether young, growing, mature non producing, or mature producing, as studied in the previous two lessons. Checking the correct quantity means avoiding both underfeeding, which can slow growth or reduce production, and overfeeding, which can waste feed or cause health problems such as excessive weight gain. Ensuring clean feeding equipment, such as troughs, feeders and water containers, helps prevent the spread of disease between animals.

pages.title: The Feeding Process
pages.body:
Approaching the animal calmly, placing feed in the correct location, observing the animal while it feeds, and providing clean water are four steps that make up the core feeding process for most domestic and commercial animals. Approaching animals calmly and consistently helps avoid startling them, which is especially important with animals that are easily frightened or that may react defensively. Placing feed in the correct location, such as a clean trough or feeder rather than directly on the ground, reduces contamination and waste. Observing the animal while it feeds allows a farmer to notice early signs of illness, such as reduced appetite or unusual behaviour. Providing clean water alongside feed is essential, since water supports digestion and all other body processes, and an animal with plenty of feed but insufficient water will still struggle to remain healthy.

[[pic:A sequence of four small illustrations showing correct feeding practice, first a farmer checking a written feed schedule against an animal's age, then the farmer pouring measured feed into a clean trough, then the farmer standing calmly nearby observing chickens or goats feeding, and finally the farmer refilling a nearby water container.]]

Notice how each step in the sequence reflects the underlying knowledge developed earlier in this strand, choosing the correct feed and quantity, and reflects safe, careful practice, calm handling, clean equipment and attentive observation.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Feeding Animals at Different Stages of Growth and Production

pages.title: Feeding Animals at Different Stages of Growth and Production
pages.body: Applying what was learnt in Lesson 10, a farmer performing feeding tasks needs to adjust both the type of feed and, often, the frequency of feeding according to an animal's stage. Young animals, such as chicks or piglets, are typically fed smaller amounts more frequently throughout the day, since their small stomachs cannot hold a large single meal, while mature animals are usually fed larger amounts less frequently. Producing animals, such as laying hens or lactating animals, may need feed available almost constantly, or at carefully timed intervals, to support their higher nutritional demands.

pages.title: Safety and Good Practice When Feeding Animals
pages.body: Washing hands before and after handling animals or feed, wearing appropriate protective clothing where necessary, and avoiding contact between sick and healthy animals during feeding are important safety practices for anyone performing animal feeding tasks. These practices protect both the person feeding the animals and the animals themselves from the spread of disease, and they reflect the kind of responsible, careful attitude expected of anyone working in agriculture.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

On larger commercial farms, feeding is often scheduled precisely and recorded formally, sometimes using automated feeding systems for very large poultry or pig operations, while on a smallholder farm or school farm, the same underlying principles, correct feed, correct quantity, calm handling, and attentive observation, are usually carried out manually. Practising these skills on a school farm gives learners direct, transferable experience relevant to both small and larger scale animal production.

questions.q: Young animals such as chicks are typically fed
questions.e: Young animals, such as chicks or piglets, are typically fed smaller amounts more frequently throughout the day, since their small stomachs cannot hold a large single meal, while mature animals are usually fed larger amounts less frequently.

questions.q: Producing animals such as laying hens often need
o: Feed available almost constantly or at carefully timed intervals
Less feed than any other animal category
No feed on days they lay eggs
Only water with no solid feed
questions.e: Producing animals, such as laying hens or lactating animals, may need feed available almost constantly, or at carefully timed intervals, to support their higher nutritional demands.

questions.q: Sick animals should generally be kept
o: Away from healthy animals during feeding
Fed with exactly the same equipment as healthy animals with no precautions
In direct contact with healthy animals at all times
Without any special consideration at all
questions.e: Washing hands before and after handling animals or feed, wearing appropriate protective clothing where necessary, and avoiding contact between sick and healthy animals during feeding are important safety practices for anyone performing animal feeding tasks.

questions.q: Prepared animal feed mainly allows a farmer to
o: Control the quality and balance of nutrients an animal receives
Increase the animal's need for water only
Prevent the animal from growing at all
Remove all responsibility for animal care
questions.e: Preparing feed deliberately, using known ingredients and a consistent method, allows a farmer to control the quality and balance of nutrients an animal receives, rather than relying only on whatever happens to be available.

questions.q: Poultry mash commonly includes ingredients such as
o: Maize bran, fish meal and soybean meal
Only water with no solid ingredients
questions.e: Poultry feed mainly on concentrated feed such as maize bran, fish meal and formulated poultry mash, alongside mineral supplements such as oyster shell to support eggshell formation in laying birds.

questions.q: Silage is prepared mainly by
o: Boiling plant material for several hours
Leaving crop residues out in the open air
Packing chopped plant material tightly to ferment

questions.q: Fish meal supplement is prepared by
o: Drying and grinding fish or fish waste

questions.q: Kitchen and farm waste feed is commonly prepared for
questions.e: Pigs are the most common monogastric livestock kept in Ghana.

questions.q: Which of the following is a general step in preparing most animal feeds?
o: Preventing any storage of the feed
Selecting ingredients randomly with no purpose
questions.e: Measuring proportions accurately ensures the feed is properly balanced rather than accidentally too rich in one nutrient and deficient in another.

questions.q: Storing finished feed in a dry, sealed container mainly helps to
o: Guarantee the feed never runs out
Protect the feed from spoiling or losing nutritional value
Remove all nutrients from the feed
questions.e: Storing the finished feed correctly, usually in a dry, sealed, pest free container, protects it from spoiling or losing nutritional value before it is used.

questions.q: Formulating feed for laying hens should particularly emphasise
questions.e: A farmer formulating feed for laying hens, for example, needs to include enough calcium to support strong eggshells, alongside adequate protein and energy, while feed formulated for a young, growing pig needs to emphasise protein for muscle development.

questions.q: Formulating feed for a young, growing pig should particularly emphasise
o: Calcium only, with no other nutrients
questions.e: A farmer formulating feed for laying hens, for example, needs to include enough calcium to support strong eggshells, alongside adequate protein and energy, while feed formulated for a young, growing pig needs to emphasise protein for muscle development.

questions.q: Commercial feed mills mainly differ from smallholder feed preparation in that they
o: Avoid using any ingredients at all
Use exactly the same tools as smallholder farmers
Use precise formulas and industrial equipment at a larger scale
questions.e: Commercial feed mills use precise formulas, often developed by animal nutritionists, and industrial equipment to prepare large quantities of consistent, balanced feed for sale to farmers.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a monogastric animal?
Ruminant animals are best described as having
o: A specialised, multi chambered stomach for digesting fibrous material
The same digestive system as poultry
questions.e: A ruminant is an animal with a specialised, multi chambered stomach that allows it to digest large amounts of fibrous plant material efficiently, through a process involving regurgitating and re chewing partly digested food, commonly called chewing the cud.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a ruminant?
questions.e: Cattle, goats and sheep are common ruminants kept in Ghana.

questions.q: Ruminants mainly feed on
o: Pure water with no solid feed
Roughage such as grass and hay
questions.e: Ruminants feed mainly on roughage, such as grass, hay, maize stalks and other fibrous crop residues, since their specialised stomach allows them to extract nutrients from this fibrous material far more effectively than other animals can.

questions.q: A monogastric animal has
o: The same stomach structure as a ruminant
questions.e: A monogastric animal has a single chambered stomach, similar in basic structure to the human stomach, which cannot break down fibrous plant material as efficiently as a ruminant's stomach can.

questions.q: Poultry digestion is supported by an organ called the
questions.e: Poultry, including chickens, guinea fowl and ducks, also have a simple digestive system, supported by a muscular organ called the gizzard that helps grind food, sometimes with the help of small stones the bird deliberately swallows.

questions.q: Compared with ruminant feed, monogastric and poultry feed is generally
o: Higher in fibre and lower in protein
Lower in fibre but higher in energy and protein
questions.e: Monogastric and poultry feed, being mainly concentrates, is generally lower in fibre but higher in energy and protein, suited to a digestive system that processes feed more quickly and needs nutrients in a more readily available form.

questions.q: Which feed characteristic is generally highest in ruminant feed compared with monogastric feed?
questions.e: Fibre content, energy content, and protein content are three characteristics that differ noticeably between the feeds typically given to ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.

questions.q: Maize bran can be used as feed for
o: Only cattle, with no other use
Only poultry, with no other use
Ruminants, monogastrics and poultry, in different proportions
questions.e: Compare and contrast the characteristics of different kinds of feed commonly consumed by categories of domestic and commercial animals, namely ruminants, monogastrics and poultry.

questions.q: Recording feed use over time mainly helps a farmer to
o: Monitor costs and detect early signs of illness
Remove the need for feed entirely
questions.e: Recording the type and amount of feed given to farm animals over a period of time, such as daily or weekly, helps a farmer track feeding costs, monitor whether animals are receiving a consistent, balanced diet, and identify problems early if an animal's feed…

questions.q: The underlying pattern across ruminants, monogastrics and poultry regarding growth stage feeding is that
o: All animals need identical feed regardless of stage
Nutritional needs change with growth stage across all these animal categories
Only poultry require different feed at different stages
Only ruminants require different feed at different stages
questions.e: Formulating feed means deliberately calculating and combining ingredients to meet the specific nutritional needs of a particular animal at a particular stage of growth, rather than simply mixing whatever ingredients are available.

questions.q: Young animals mainly need feed with a high proportion of
o: Protein, to support rapid tissue growth
Water only, with no solid feed
questions.e: Growing animals continue to rely on tissue building, but increasingly need feed to support broader development, including bone and muscle growth, in a more balanced way.

questions.q: A growing animal's feed should mainly provide
o: A balanced supply of protein and energy
Only fibre with no other nutrients
Only minerals with no protein or energy
questions.e: Selecting the right ingredients means choosing materials that supply the nutrients a particular animal needs, considering factors such as protein, energy, minerals and vitamins.

questions.q: A mature, non producing animal generally needs
o: Maximum possible protein at all times
questions.e: In general, young animals need the most protein for building tissue, growing animals need protein and energy, and mature animals need feed for maintenance, with extra nutrients when they are producing eggs, milk or young.

questions.q: A mature, producing animal such as a laying hen needs extra
o: Calcium and other nutrients to support egg production
questions.e: A mature dairy cow, a mature sow, and a mature laying hen all need extra nutrients to support production, though again the specific feed differs, a lactation ration rich in energy for the cow, a lactation feed for the sow, and a calcium enriched layer feed…

questions.q: Grower feed is typically given to
questions.e: Notice how the type of feed changes at each stage to match the animal's changing needs, moving from a strong emphasis on protein while young, through a balanced feed while growing, to a feed enriched with minerals such as calcium once the animal begins laying…

questions.q: Layer feed is specifically formulated for
questions.e: Notice how the type of feed changes at each stage to match the animal's changing needs, moving from a strong emphasis on protein while young, through a balanced feed while growing, to a feed enriched with minerals such as calcium once the animal begins laying…

questions.q: Overfeeding a mature, non producing animal relative to its needs can lead to
o: Guaranteed improved health with no drawbacks
No effect on the animal at all
questions.e: Overfeeding or underfeeding an animal relative to its growth stage can cause real problems, such as excessive fat deposits in an overfed, mature, non producing animal, or poor growth and weakened immunity in an underfed young animal.

questions.q: Starter feed is typically given to
o: Only ruminants and never poultry or pigs
Young animals such as chicks, calves or piglets
questions.e: Young animals, such as chicks or piglets, are typically fed smaller amounts more frequently throughout the day, since their small stomachs cannot hold a large single meal, while mature animals are usually fed larger amounts less frequently.

questions.q: Underfeeding a young, growing animal can lead to
o: No effect on the animal at all
questions.e: Overfeeding or underfeeding an animal relative to its growth stage can cause real problems, such as excessive fat deposits in an overfed, mature, non producing animal, or poor growth and weakened immunity in an underfed young animal.

questions.q: Before feeding an animal, a farmer should first
o: Confirm the feed matches the animal's category and growth stage
Feed as much as possible regardless of the animal's needs
Ignore the type of feed being used
Use any available feed without checking it
questions.e: Confirming the correct feed means checking that the feed matches both the animal's digestive category, ruminant, monogastric or poultry, and its specific growth stage, whether young, growing, mature non producing, or mature producing, as studied in the…

questions.q: Checking the correct feed quantity mainly helps to avoid
o: Guaranteed weight loss in all animals
Preventing the animal from eating at all
Removing the need for any feed
questions.e: Checking the correct quantity means avoiding both underfeeding, which can slow growth or reduce production, and overfeeding, which can waste feed or cause health problems such as excessive weight gain.

questions.q: Clean feeding equipment mainly helps to
o: Guarantee faster growth with no other input
Increase the risk of disease spread
Prevent the spread of disease between animals
Remove the need for feed entirely
questions.e: Ensuring clean feeding equipment, such as troughs, feeders and water containers, helps prevent the spread of disease between animals.

questions.q: Approaching animals calmly during feeding mainly helps to
o: Avoid startling or frightening the animal
Guarantee the animal will produce more offspring
Prevent the animal from eating at all
questions.e: Approaching animals calmly and consistently helps avoid startling them, which is especially important with animals that are easily frightened or that may react defensively.

questions.q: Observing an animal while it feeds can help a farmer to
o: Guarantee the animal never becomes ill
Notice early signs of illness such as reduced appetite
Prevent the animal from drinking water
Remove the need for any further care
questions.e: Observing the animal while it feeds allows a farmer to notice early signs of illness, such as reduced appetite or unusual behaviour.

questions.q: Providing clean water alongside feed is important because
o: Water has no role in digestion
Water is unnecessary if enough feed is given
Water should always be withheld during feeding
Water supports digestion and other body processes
questions.e: Providing clean water alongside feed is essential, since water supports digestion and all other body processes, and an animal with plenty of feed but insufficient water will still struggle to remain healthy.

o: Reduce the risk of spreading disease
Remove the need for clean equipment
